draft.title: Framing a research question
card: A research question is the one question an investigation sets out to answer. It starts the whole investigation, and every later step follows from it.
A good question can be tested with data. This means the answer can be found by measuring or counting something, such as sprint times or the number of push-ups.
A clear question names what is being changed and what is being measured. For example: does a five-minute warm-up change 40 m sprint times in Year 11 students?

A question that asks for an opinion or a value judgement, such as which sport is best, cannot be settled by data alone. A group also needs a question it can realistically test with the time and equipment it has.
draft.remember: A good research question is clear and can be answered by measuring or counting something.

a.q: Which of these is the best research question for a group to investigate?
opts: Does stretching for 5 minutes change sit-and-reach scores?
Is stretching a good thing for young people to do?
Should schools make students stretch before sport?
Why do people enjoy stretching so much?
a.why: The first question names what changes (stretching) and what is measured (sit-and-reach scores), so data can answer it. The second is tempting, but good is a value judgement that measurements cannot settle.
a.clue: Which question names something you could measure?

b.q: Priya's group wants to study sleep and netball. Which question is clearest and most testable with data?
opts: Do players who sleep 8 hours score more goals than 6 hours?
Is sleep the most important thing for netball players?
Should netball teams make players go to bed early?
Do netball players know enough about sleep?
b.why: The first question names the sleep amounts being compared and a measurable result, goals scored. The second sounds scientific, but most important is a judgement, and the other options are about opinions or what people should do.
b.clue: Look for the question that names what is compared and what is counted.

a.best: Does stretching for 5 minutes change sit-and-reach scores?

b.best: Do players who sleep 8 hours score more goals than 6 hours?

problems.detail: The right option is ungrammatical: 'score more goals than 6 hours' compares players with hours. It should read 'than players who sleep 6 hours'.
The right option is clearly the longest and the only one with precise numbers (8 hours, 6 hours, goals), so a student can spot it without knowing the idea.
The right option is the only one with precise, measurable detail (5 minutes, sit-and-reach scores), so it stands out from the vaguer distractors.

b.q: Priya's group wants to study sleep and netball. Which question is clearest and most testable with data?
